messages.author: 1f723d378f24adbb
messages.subject: conceptual question: truncated model & Jacobian
parts:
Hi,

This is a simplified, self-contained example of a part a model which I
am trying to formulate. I am assuming that I am making a conceptual
mistake somewhere, since the posterior does not resemble the data, but I
don't know where.

The data generating process is

N <- 100
w <- rlnorm(N,0,1)
a <- runif(N,0,1)
m <- 2
keep <- w < a*m
w_kept <- w[keep]
a_kept <- a[keep]
N_kept <- sum(keep)

in other words, w is lognormal, a is uniform, observations are kept when
w < a*m. m is assumed to be known.

The Stan program I wrote is

data {
int<lower=1> N_kept;
real m;
}
parameters {
vector<lower=0,upper=1>[N_kept] a_kept;
vector<lower=0,upper=1>[N_kept] b;
}
model {
vector[N_kept] w_kept;
for (i in 1:N_kept) {
w_kept[i] <- b[i]*a_kept[i];
}
increment_log_prob(log(a_kept));
a_kept ~ uniform(0,1);
w_kept ~ lognormal(0,1);
}

I think that the log det of the Jacobian is log(a_kept[i]) for each
observation. I know I could integrate out b[i] but I am trying to
understand the problem first, which is the following: the posterior
means of a_kept are clustered around 0.7, nothing resembling the data.

It would be really great if someone could point out the source of the
error.

Best,

Tamas

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] conceptual question: truncated model & Jacobian
parts:
I was only looking at Jonah's comments and missed the part where
you explained you added the Jacobian.

> data {
> int<lower=1> N_kept;
> real m;
> }
> parameters {
> vector<lower=0,upper=1>[N_kept] a_kept;
> vector<lower=0,upper=1>[N_kept] b;
> }
> model {
> vector[N_kept] w_kept;
> for (i in 1:N_kept) {
> w_kept[i] <- b[i]*a_kept[i];
> }
> increment_log_prob(log(a_kept));
> a_kept ~ uniform(0,1);
> w_kept ~ lognormal(0,1);

It's very neatly done, too, because log is vectorized as is increment_log_prob.

You could also write the model just as:

increment_log_prob(log(a_kept));
(b .* a_kept) ~ lognormal(0, 1);

You can then ignore the Jacobian warning.

The uniform(0, 1) is redundant given that you have
the constraint on a_kept.

I don't think the lognormal adds much given that w_kept is
in (0, 1) and lognormal(0, 1) has a mean of roughly 2 and
an sd of roughly 6.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] conceptual question: truncated model & Jacobian
parts:
Now I think that the following is happening: there is no reason for the
posterior _means_ of a_kept to match the simulated data. Only the
_distribution_ should match.

A graph which shows both is attached, plotting & other code at
https://gist.github.com/tpapp/66efec47df7710062096

If someone could confirm that what I am saying makes sense that would be
really useful.

Also, in general, I am curious what approach people use for testing
models (which are non-trivial and need testing for programming errors,
eg Jacobians, etc --- this is part of such a model). So far I have been
simulating data and eyeballing the scatterplots of posterior means vs
data, which got me into trouble here. On the other end of the spectrum
is the self-cleaning oven (Cook, Gelman, and Rubin), but that is
time-consuming, especially when I develop models iteratively in Stan. Is
there anything else in between?

Best,

Tamas

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] conceptual question: truncated model & Jacobian
parts:
Here's an example that might be useful. Suppose I know
the data y come from a normal(mu, 1) distribution so that
the true model is

y ~ normal(mu, 1)

Now suppose I draw

y[1], y[2], y[3] ~ normal(0, 1).

I might get -1.5, -1.8, +0.3, so that the MLE is

mu* = -1

That's why there's no reason to expect the posterior mode
to be equal to the true value.

So what you need to do is a bunch of simulations and see
if the posterior intervals have the proper coverage. That is,
will the true value be in the posterior 80% interval around
80% of the time? The in-between approach if you have a lot of
parameters is to make sure 80% of the parameter estimates are
in their posterior 80% intervals.

For this case (and most others), in the limit as N -> infinity,
then the posterior mean and mode both approach the true value
(here mu = 0). The standard error's going to shrink as 1/sqrt(N).

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] conceptual question: truncated model & Jacobian
parts:
First step is to choose random (put reasonable) true
values, simulate data, then fit that simulated data to
ensure that the posterior covers the “true” values
reasonable well. Compare parameters to parameters.

If you want to look at the data then you have to sample
from the posterior predictive distribution and then compare
measured data to simulated data (i.e. posterior predictive
checks).

In general parameters and data have no relation.
